items.prompt: Why is a team's agreement that its own button is obvious weak evidence?
choices: Team opinions about layout and colour are almost always wrong in practice
They know what it means, so they cannot see it as a newcomer does
Five people is too small a group to hold a shared opinion at all
items.explanation: The builders' knowledge is exactly what a first-time user lacks, so their agreement says little about newcomers.

items.prompt: What does the curse of knowledge describe?
choices: Once you know something, it is hard to imagine not knowing it
Designers lose their creativity after studying one design for too long
Users forget instructions faster than designers do
items.explanation: It names the blind spot: you cannot easily simulate being a person who does not know.

items.prompt: Which method watches what people actually do on a task?
choices: A customer survey
A team vote
A usability test
items.explanation: A survey records what people say; a usability test records behaviour.

items.prompt: Who should attempt the tasks in a usability test?
choices: The designers who built it, so they can explain it
Any teammate who has some spare time
Realistic people who did not build the design
items.explanation: Only people who do not already know the design can show whether it explains itself.

items.prompt: What do participants receive when they start a task?
choices: A goal to reach, but no instructions on how to reach it
Step-by-step directions to follow carefully, one screen at a time
A guided tour of the whole design, given just before the task begins
items.explanation: Giving the path would hide whether the design shows the path by itself.

items.prompt: Do you need hundreds of participants to learn something useful?
choices: Yes, below a hundred people the results are random noise
No, a handful already reveals the biggest problems
Yes, otherwise nobody inside the company will believe the results
items.explanation: Common problems show up repeatedly, so even a small group surfaces most of them.

items.prompt: Which of these is an observation rather than an opinion?
choices: Two people tapped the trash icon first
I think the layout looks clean and calm
Most of us like the new header a lot
items.explanation: An observation describes what a person did; the others describe how someone feels.

items.prompt: Why do what people say they would do and what they do often differ?
choices: People usually lie to researchers on purpose to look good
People remember every design perfectly but ignore their tasks
People predict their behaviour poorly until a real task arrives
items.explanation: Prediction and action use different thinking, so only action is trustworthy evidence.

items.prompt: A team of five unanimously calls its new settings page 'clear' and skips testing. What is the core flaw in that reasoning?
choices: Unanimity among only five people is statistically too weak a signal to count
Settings pages are too complex for any internal reviewer to judge fairly
Their familiarity means their agreement predicts nothing about newcomers
Internal reviews happen too early in a project to be informative at all
items.explanation: Their shared knowledge is exactly what newcomers lack. Group size and timing are not the issue; the audience is.
items.reference:
Opinion versus observation
🗳️ team vote: shows what the team believes
📋 survey: shows what people say they would do
👀 usability test: shows what people actually do
🧠 curse of knowledge: builders cannot unsee the meaning
Why: agreement among people who know the design predicts nothing about people who do not.
items.learnMore:
Evidence has to come from someone who does not already know the answer

A design's builders carry knowledge a newcomer lacks, so their confidence is a fact about the builders. Watching a few realistic strangers attempt a real task is the cheapest way to get evidence that is about the users.

Common mistake

Treating a unanimous team review as if it were a test.
items.reflection: Think of an instruction or sign you wrote that seemed perfectly clear to you. Who could you have watched trying it, and what might you have seen?

items.prompt: A survey says 90% of 200 customers found checkout 'easy', yet only 2 of 6 people in a usability test finished it unaided. How should the team read this?
choices: The test records real behaviour, so it better shows whether checkout works
The survey wins because its sample is far larger than the test's sample
Both measure the same thing, so one of them must hold a recording error
The six test participants must be unusual, so their result should be dropped
items.explanation: The survey records impressions; the test records what people did. They answer different questions, and only one answers 'can people complete it?'.

items.prompt: Which finding could only come from watching people attempt a task?
choices: Customers rate the page 4 out of 5 on average across the survey
Most customers told us they prefer the blue colour theme over the grey
The team likes the new logo more than the old logo they replaced
Three people tapped a decorative banner, taking it for the buy button
items.explanation: A banner mistaken for a button is a behaviour. The others are ratings and preferences that no one needed to watch to collect.

items.prompt: A designer says, 'After months of work I'm sure a stranger will get this in five seconds.' What is the best next step?
choices: Poll three more teammates until the answer is unanimous
Have a few strangers try a real task while someone watches
Write a longer rationale explaining why the layout works
Ship it and read the support tickets that arrive afterwards
items.explanation: Only observation of strangers can confirm or refute the prediction; more insiders or more prose adds no new evidence.

items.prompt: What is task success rate?
choices: The share of participants who said they liked the task afterwards
The share of participants who finish a task correctly and unaided
The average time all participants spent working on the task overall
items.explanation: It counts clean completions out of everyone who attempted the task.

items.prompt: Three of six participants completed a task unaided. What is the rate?
items.explanation: 3 divided by 6 is 0.5, so 50%.

items.prompt: The moderator helps a participant finish the task. How is it scored?
choices: As a failure
As a success
As half a success
items.explanation: Help means the design did not carry the participant through on its own.

items.prompt: What is the think-aloud protocol?
choices: The moderator explains the design out loud to participants
The team reads the session notes out loud afterwards
Participants narrate their thoughts out loud while working
items.explanation: Narration exposes the reasoning behind each move.

items.prompt: A participant finishes the task by luck after visible struggle. What is that outcome called?
choices: A clean, plain success
A failure to attempt
A flagged success
items.explanation: The task got done, but the struggle is a warning that the design is unclear.

items.prompt: Why does the definition include the word 'unaided'?
choices: Help would hide the very confusion the test is meant to catch
Unaided sessions are shorter and cheaper to run for the team
Participants usually prefer to work without anyone helping them
items.explanation: If the moderator supplies the missing knowledge, the result no longer describes the design.

items.prompt: How many outcomes does the unit describe for a task?
choices: Two: simply pass and fail, since nothing lies in between them
Three: success, failure and flagged success
Five: one for each severity level
items.explanation: The third outcome exists because finishing is not always understanding.

items.prompt: Four of five participants complete a task unaided. What is the rate?
items.explanation: 4 divided by 5 is 0.8, so 80%.

items.prompt: A participant says 'I have no idea what this does, I'll click it... oh, that worked' and finishes the task. How should it be scored?
choices: Clean success, because the task was completed correctly and unaided
Failure, because the participant never really understood the design
Discard the session, because narrating aloud contaminated the result
Success, flagged: it was unaided, but the narration shows guesswork
items.explanation: Completion was real, but the words show the design did not explain itself, so the success carries a flag.
items.reference:
Scoring one task
✅ correct and unaided: success
❌ gave up, or the moderator had to help: failure
⚠️ done by luck or after visible struggle: flagged
➗ rate = clean successes ÷ participants
Why: the unaided requirement is what makes the number a statement about the design.
items.learnMore:
A rate is only as honest as its scoring rules

Counting a task as done only when it was correct and unaided makes the percentage comparable between rounds. Think-aloud narration tells you whether a finished task was understanding or a lucky guess.

Common mistake

Counting every finished task as a clean success.
items.reflection: Pick a task you help others learn. How would you tell a person who understood it from one who got lucky?

items.prompt: Eight participants attempt a task: 5 finish unaided, 1 finishes after a moderator hint, 2 give up. What is the task success rate?
choices: 6 of 8, which is 75%
5 of 8, which is 62.5%
7 of 8, which is 87.5%
2 of 8, which is 25%
items.explanation: The hinted finish counts as a failure, so only the 5 unaided completions count: 5 / 8 = 62.5%.

items.prompt: Two rounds both show 4 of 6 succeeding, but round 2's narration is full of doubt. What does that illustrate?
choices: The same rate can hide different causes, which only narration reveals
Think-aloud makes participants less likely to succeed on later tasks
The second round should simply have used far more participants
Success rate is meaningless unless it eventually reaches one hundred percent
items.explanation: A number summarises outcomes; the narration explains how people reached them.

items.prompt: Which result would mislead a team that checks only whether the task got done?
choices: Only 2 of 6 finish, and all four others say what blocked them
None of the 6 finish, and everyone says the same thing
All 6 finish, but 4 admit they were guessing the whole way
5 of 6 finish, and the one failure was a hardware fault
items.explanation: Completion hides the guessing. The other results are already visible failures or have an explained cause.

items.prompt: What should a good usability task state?
choices: The exact buttons to press, one after another, in order
The team's view of the best route
A goal to reach, never the path to reach it
items.explanation: A goal lets the participant show whether the design reveals the path.

items.prompt: Which task states only a goal?
choices: Click the menu, then tap Settings
Turn off email notifications
Tap the bell icon and switch it off
items.explanation: The other two name controls, which leaks the path.

items.prompt: Why does a task need a clear finish line?
choices: So sessions always end within five minutes
So observers can score success or failure the same way
So participants know exactly when to stop narrating aloud
items.explanation: A visible end state makes scoring consistent.

items.prompt: Which task has an observable finish line?
choices: Turn off email notifications
Explore the settings page for a while
Get a general feel for the whole app
items.explanation: Notifications either are off or are not; exploring has no end state.

items.prompt: Why is 'Tap the cart icon, then tap checkout' a poor task?
choices: It is too long for participants to remember accurately
It asks for more than one tap in a row
It reveals what the design itself was meant to show
items.explanation: Telling people which icon is the cart removes the thing being tested.

items.prompt: Asking 'What do you think of this page?' mostly gets you what?
choices: Behaviour you can watch fail
A scored success or failure
Opinions about how it looks
items.explanation: Opinions are not behaviour and cannot be scored.

items.prompt: Which task is best for testing product search?
choices: Find a pair of blue shoes to buy
Use the search bar to look up 'blue shoes'
Tell me about the shoe page
items.explanation: It names the goal without naming the search bar.

items.prompt: In what words should a task be written?
choices: The labels the team uses inside the interface itself, word for word
Plain words describing the user's goal, not the interface's labels
Technical terms so participants take the session seriously
items.explanation: Interface labels would hint at what to look for on the screen.

items.prompt: Which prompt best tests whether people can find the returns policy?
choices: Click Help, then Returns, and read the whole policy page carefully
Look around the Help area and tell me what you think of it
You bought the wrong size; find out whether you can send it back
Find the Returns link in the page footer and open it up
items.explanation: It states a realistic goal with a visible end and names no control. The footer prompt leaks the path.
items.reference:
A task worth testing
🎯 goal: 'Turn off email notifications'
🚫 path: 'Open the menu, then tap Settings'
🏁 finish line: a state an observer can see
🧩 plain words, not the interface's labels
Why: a path tells participants the answer the test exists to find out whether the design gives.
items.learnMore:
State the goal, never the route

A good task names what the person wants and when it is done. Anything that names a control or a menu leaks the information the design is supposed to provide by itself.

Common mistake

Writing steps that sound helpful but give away where things are.
items.reflection: Think of directions you gave someone. Which parts told them where to go instead of what to find, and what did that hide?

items.prompt: A team writes the task 'Explore the account page'. What scoring problem does it create?
choices: With no defined end state, two observers can disagree on success
Participants will finish too quickly to have time to narrate anything
Exploration tasks always produce a success rate of exactly one hundred percent
The moderator will be tempted to explain the page far too early
items.explanation: Without an observable finish, success becomes a matter of opinion.

items.prompt: A team rewrites 'Tap Add to cart' as 'Buy two of these'. What does the rewrite improve?
choices: It makes the task longer, which slows participants down a lot
It guarantees that every participant will now complete the purchase
It tests participants' memory of the whole shop's product catalogue
It no longer names the control, so findability is what gets tested
items.explanation: Removing the control's name turns a command into a goal.

items.prompt: The task says 'Use the new Quick Pay feature to pay.' Why is that risky?
choices: Payment tasks are too sensitive to include in any usability test at all
The team's invented label gives away a name users may not recognise
The word 'new' will make participants anxious about making errors
Feature names are always too short for participants to understand
items.explanation: If real users would not know that name, using it hides a possible failure.

items.prompt: What is the moderator's main job during a task?
choices: Watch quietly and let the participant work
Explain each screen as the participant reaches it
Correct wrong taps immediately and kindly
items.explanation: Silence lets the design be the only guide.

items.prompt: A participant goes silent. What should the moderator say?
choices: Try the icon over there in the corner
No, that is not the right one at all
What are you thinking right now?
items.explanation: A neutral prompt restarts narration without giving information.

items.prompt: What happens to a task result if the moderator gives a hint?
choices: It becomes more reliable as evidence overall
It no longer measures the design unaided
It counts as double the evidence
items.explanation: The hint replaces what the design should have communicated.

items.prompt: How often should the task be stated?
choices: Again each minute
Once, in plain language
After every click, to keep people on track
items.explanation: Repeating it shapes the participant's attention and adds hints.

items.prompt: What does think-aloud give you that silent pass/fail does not?
choices: The reason for a stall, not just that it happened
A guarantee that every participant will succeed
A shorter session with less work for the moderator
items.explanation: Narration exposes the misreading behind the failure.

items.prompt: How should a moderator handle the urge to help a struggling participant?
choices: Give a small hint so the session stays pleasant
End the task and move on to the next one
Resist it, because the struggle is the evidence
items.explanation: Helping erases the evidence the session exists to gather.

items.prompt: A participant gives up. What do you record?
choices: Nothing, because the session is invalid
A success, for the effort
A failure, and where they stopped
items.explanation: Giving up is a valid and informative outcome.

items.prompt: A participant asks 'Is this right?' What is the best reply?
choices: What would you expect to happen?
Yes, that is exactly the correct one
No, try the other tab on the left
items.explanation: Turning the question back keeps the moderator neutral.

items.prompt: A participant hovers silently over the screen for 20 seconds. What is the best moderator move?
choices: Point to the area of the screen where the control sits
Say that most people find it in the top-right menu
End the task and score it as a failure at once
Ask neutrally what they are thinking right now
items.explanation: A neutral question restarts narration; pointing or hinting would leak the answer.
items.reference:
What a moderator does
🗣️ states the task once, in plain words
🤫 stays quiet while the participant works
❓ if silent: asks 'what are you thinking?'
🚫 gives no hints, even small ones
Why: any hint supplies what the design should have supplied.
items.learnMore:
Struggle is the data

The moderator's discipline is what keeps the session about the design. A neutral prompt keeps the participant talking; a hint changes what is being measured.

Common mistake

Helping because watching someone struggle feels unkind.
items.reflection: When did you last explain something to a person who was struggling? What might you have learned by staying quiet a little longer?

items.prompt: Which moderator remark leaves the data cleanest?
choices: Most people use the menu icon here
What are you looking for right now?
Have you tried the tab on the left?
Good, that is the correct button
items.explanation: Only the first adds no information about the design; the others hint or confirm.

items.prompt: Why does a small hint damage a result as much as a large one?
choices: Both supply information the design should have provided itself
Small hints are remembered much longer than large hints are
Participants stop narrating entirely once they receive any hint
Only large hints change the score recorded on paper
items.explanation: The line is crossed at any hint: the task then measures obedience, not the design.

items.prompt: What does a narrated failure add compared with a silent one?
choices: It lowers the number of failures in the final count
It lets the moderator step in with a quicker fix sooner
It exposes the misreading, so the fix can target it
It turns every recorded failure into a flagged success
items.explanation: Narration explains the cause; it does not change the outcome.

items.prompt: What does a severity rating help a team decide?
choices: Which participants to invite next time
What to fix first
How long the next session should last
items.explanation: Severity turns a list of failures into a fix order.

items.prompt: What is a cosmetic problem?
choices: Noticed and mildly annoying, but it does not block the task
A problem that blocks the task for most participants
A problem that only the moderator happens to notice later on
items.explanation: Cosmetic problems do not stop anyone.

items.prompt: Which is usually more severe?
choices: A button colour that looks slightly off-brand
A label that some people find dull
A problem that blocks the purchase
items.explanation: Blocking the core goal outranks looking off-brand.

items.prompt: Which two questions shape severity?
choices: How long the fix takes, and who first found it
How many people hit it, and what it costs them
How much the page weighs, and how it looks overall
items.explanation: Frequency and consequence together set severity.

items.prompt: Is 'easy to fix' the same as 'worth fixing first'?
choices: Yes, easy fixes always come first
No, they are two different rankings
Yes, but only for cosmetic problems
items.explanation: Severity keeps a team from optimising for ease by accident.

items.prompt: What is a minor problem?
choices: It slows people down, but all of them recover unaided
It blocks the task for about half of participants
It risks real harm to participants during the study session
items.explanation: Minor problems cost time, not success.

items.prompt: What is a critical problem?
choices: It was reported by the oldest participant
It is the first problem the moderator wrote down
It blocks most people and blocks the core goal
items.explanation: Critical combines wide reach with a blocked goal.

items.prompt: All 6 participants hesitated on 'Add to cart' but all succeeded. What severity is that?
choices: Critical
Cosmetic
Minor
items.explanation: It slowed them, they recovered, and everyone completed the task.

items.prompt: Problem A: 5 of 6 could not find an optional gift-wrap option. Problem B: 3 of 6 could not complete payment. Which first?
choices: A, because it affects more of the participants overall in this study
Neither, until a larger group has been tested to confirm it
B, because it blocks the core goal even though fewer people hit it
A, because optional features reach a bigger audience than payment
items.explanation: Consequence matters as much as reach, and payment is the core goal.
items.reference:
Ranking what to fix
🎨 cosmetic: noticed, does not block
🐌 minor: slows people, all recover
🚧 major: blocks many, goal still reachable
🛑 critical: blocks most, blocks the core goal
Why: severity weighs how many people hit a problem and what it costs them.
items.learnMore:
Easy to fix is not the same as worth fixing first

A fix order needs two inputs: how many participants were affected and whether the problem stops the person reaching the goal. The cheapest fix is a separate ranking from the most severe one.

Common mistake

Fixing the quick wins first and calling the list handled.
items.reflection: Look at a list of small and large problems in your own work. Which one are you tempted to fix first only because it is easy?

items.prompt: Promo code and checkout both failed for 4 of 6 participants. Why are they rated differently?
choices: Skipping the promo still allows a purchase; failing checkout does not
Checkout failures are always rated higher because they come last in the flow
Promo codes are used by too few shoppers to deserve a rating
The checkout failures happened later in the session than the promo-code ones
items.explanation: Equal reach, different consequence.

items.prompt: Assume each participant has a 31% chance of surfacing a given problem. What is that chance for one participant?
items.explanation: The assumption is the per-participant chance, here 31%.

items.prompt: What shape does the problems-found curve have?
choices: It rises in a perfectly straight line forever
It rises fast at first, then flattens
It stays flat, then jumps up at the very end
items.explanation: Each participant finds less new than the one before.

items.prompt: About how many participants find roughly 84% of problems?
choices: Five
Two
Twenty

items.prompt: Which plan finds problems sooner?
choices: Fifty at once, right before launch
One participant, then wait a year
Five now, fix them, then five more
items.explanation: Rounds with fixes let you catch what the fixes missed.

items.prompt: Why do later participants add less?
choices: They are less careful than earlier ones
They mostly meet problems that earlier ones already found
The moderator gets tired and misses things as the day goes on
items.explanation: Diminishing returns come from repeats.

items.prompt: What matters before how many participants?
choices: That they are all friends of the team
That they represent real users
That they are all designers
items.explanation: More of the wrong people finds problems faster, not better.

items.prompt: Does the 31% figure apply exactly to every product?
choices: No, it is an assumption that can differ by product
Yes, it is a fixed law of nature for every single product
Yes, but only for mobile products
items.explanation: It is an estimate used here for illustration.

items.prompt: After 10 participants about 98% are found. What do 5 more add?
choices: About 15 percentage points
About 40 percentage points
About 2 percentage points
items.explanation: From about 97.6% to about 99.6% is roughly 2 points.

items.prompt: At 31% per participant, what is the chance that a given problem is missed by all of 3 participants?
choices: About 67%
About 69%
About 93%
About 33%
items.explanation: 0.69^3 is about 0.33. The 67% figure is the chance it is found at least once.
items.reference:
Small groups find most problems
📈 1 participant: about 31% of problems (assumed)
📈 5 participants: about 84%
📈 10 participants: about 98%
🔁 5 now, fix, 5 later beats 1 big study
Why: later participants mostly meet problems the earlier ones already found.
items.learnMore:
Early and often beats big and late

With an assumed 31% chance per participant, the share of problems found is 1 - 0.69^n. That climbs quickly and then flattens, so spreading the same sessions over rounds with fixes between them finds more, sooner.

Common mistake

Waiting for a large study right before launch.
items.reflection: Think of a project where you could have checked early with a few people. What would you have caught sooner?

items.prompt: A team has budget for 15 sessions. Which plan finds the most, soonest?

items.explanation: Fixes between rounds let later participants surface new problems.

items.prompt: Participant 3 found the field after 40 seconds and said 'that seems like just a summary'. How is she scored?
choices: Clean success, nothing to note
Failure, because she hesitated
Success, flagged
items.explanation: She completed it unaided but with the same confusion as the failures.

items.prompt: Counting only unflagged successes, what is the rate for the six sessions?
choices: 2 of 6, or 33%
3 of 6, or 50%
4 of 6, or 67%
items.explanation: Only participants 2 and 5 were clean.

items.prompt: Counting bare pass/fail, what is the rate?
choices: 2 of 6, or 33%
3 of 6, or 50%
1 of 6, or 17%
items.explanation: Participants 2, 3 and 5 completed the task.

items.prompt: Why act on the stricter number before launch?
choices: It shows if the design works smoothly for a first-time user
It is always higher and more encouraging
It ignores narration entirely, which makes it simpler to compute
items.explanation: Friction that patient participants overcame would make less patient customers quit.

items.prompt: Participant 4 asked the moderator for help. How is that scored?
choices: Success
Flagged success
Failure
items.explanation: Help means the task was not completed unaided.

items.prompt: What did participant 3's narration reveal?
choices: That the design was perfectly clear to her from the very start
Same confusion as three failures, which she pushed through
That she should have been excluded
items.explanation: She described the same misreading as the failures.

items.prompt: Counting participant 3, how many of the six struggled to find the field?
choices: Three
Four
Six
items.explanation: Participants 1, 3, 4 and 6 struggled.

items.prompt: What happens if a team reports only the generous number?
choices: It consistently overestimates how ready the design is
It consistently underestimates how ready the design is
It has no effect at all on the launch decision
items.explanation: Hidden friction never reaches the decision.

items.prompt: Eight sessions: 4 clean successes, 2 flagged successes, 2 failures. What are the bare and unflagged rates?
choices: 50% bare, 25% unflagged
100% bare, 50% unflagged
75% bare, 50% unflagged
75% bare, 25% unflagged
items.explanation: Bare counts 6 of 8; unflagged counts 4 of 8.
items.reference:
Two ways to count 6 sessions
✅ participants 2 and 5: clean successes
⚠️ participant 3: success, flagged (40 s hesitation)
❌ participants 1, 4, 6: failures
📊 bare pass/fail 3 of 6 = 50%; unflagged 2 of 6 = 33%
Why: the generous number answers 'did it get done', the strict one answers 'does it work smoothly'.
items.learnMore:
A success can carry a warning

Participant 3 finished on her own but said the field sounded like a summary, which is the same confusion that made three others quit. Counting only unflagged successes gives the number to act on before launch.

Common mistake

items.prompt: Why is participant 3's 40-second hesitation more important than her being counted as a success?

It proves she was a weak participant who ought to be dropped
It shows the moderator should have helped her much sooner
It proves the placement of the field is perfectly fine
items.explanation: Her words locate the cause, which a bare count would hide.

items.prompt: After moving the promo field, what should the team do?
choices: Ship it straight away because it looks better
Ask the original six whether they like it now
Re-run the same task with fresh participants
items.explanation: A re-test checks whether the one change actually helped.

items.prompt: Why use fresh participants?
choices: Fresh people are always more cooperative
Earlier participants are no longer available to the team
The earlier ones already know where the field is
items.explanation: Their success would measure memory, not the design.

items.prompt: Success rises from 33% to 83%. What does that tell you?
choices: The fix worked in aggregate
The design is perfect
The narration no longer matters
items.explanation: The aggregate improved, but narration may still show friction.

items.prompt: Why still read the narration after a good number?
choices: Because numbers are never reliable
A new kind of hesitation would only appear there
Because the moderator must justify the session afterwards
items.explanation: Counts cannot show new confusion.

items.prompt: What is wrong with using fellow designers as participants?
choices: The sample does not represent real customers
Designers are too slow at tasks
Designers flatly refuse to think aloud in sessions
items.explanation: They share the curse of knowledge.

items.prompt: Does adding more designers fix that problem?
choices: Yes, twenty designers are equal to one customer
Yes, but only when the task is made much stricter
No, the problem is who they are, not how many
items.explanation: A bigger wrong sample is still wrong.

items.prompt: What does the team have now that a room vote never produced?
choices: A unanimous opinion from everyone who built the design
A specific, defensible reason with a located cause
A faster design process with fewer review meetings
items.explanation: Observation named the cause and gave evidence for delaying.

items.prompt: Five of six participants succeed. What is the rate?
items.explanation: 5 divided by 6 is about 0.83.

items.prompt: A fresh retest has 5 of 6 succeeding, but 3 of those 5 say 'I'm not sure that was right'. What is the best decision?
choices: Ship now, because 83% proves that the design works for everyone
Revert the change because three of the participants hesitated
Ignore the comments, because only the count really matters here
It worked in aggregate, but look into the new hesitation first
items.explanation: The number improved; the narration shows a new kind of friction.
items.reference:
Closing the loop
🔧 fix the located cause
🆕 re-run the same task with fresh participants
📊 compare the success rate
🗣️ read the narration for new hesitation
Why: the number says whether the fix worked; the narration says whether anything new is wrong.
items.learnMore:
Check the fix, and who checks it

A re-test is only fair with people who have not seen the old design, and who resemble real users. The rate shows the aggregate change; narration still reveals a new kind of hesitation.

Common mistake

Re-testing with the same people or with colleagues.
